item.title: Human behaviour
item.description: Precise words for describing how and why people think, feel and act as they do.

children.definition: to keep delaying a task you should do, often doing easier things instead
children.example: I procrastinated for a week and then wrote the whole essay in one night.

children.definition: behaving in the same way as most people in a group
children.example: Teenagers often feel strong pressure towards conformity.

children.definition: too satisfied with yourself, so you stop trying to improve or notice risks
children.example: After passing the first round, the team became complacent and lost.

children.definition: the careful examination of your own thoughts and feelings
children.example: A year abroad led to a lot of introspection about what she really wanted.

children.definition: to invent sensible-sounding reasons for behaviour whose real causes are different
children.example: He rationalised the expensive purchase by calling it an investment.

children.definition: a feeling of shyness or worry that stops you from acting naturally
children.example: Speaking in a club with friendly people helped him lose his inhibitions.

children.definition: easily tricked because you believe whatever people tell you
children.example: Scammers target gullible users with fake prize messages.

children.definition: having mixed or opposite feelings about something at the same time
children.example: She's ambivalent about the job offer: the pay is good, but it means leaving home.

children.definition: the habit of following what a crowd does without thinking for yourself
children.example: Panic buying is a clear example of herd mentality.

children.definition: behaviour that damages your own chances of success, often without your realising it
children.example: Staying up late before every exam is a form of self-sabotage.

children.definition: to understand and share another person's feelings
children.example: Having moved schools often, she could empathise with the new student.

children.definition: the uncomfortable feeling of holding two beliefs, or a belief and an action, that contradict each other
children.example: Caring about the planet while flying every month can create cognitive dissonance.
